finding.claim: The /settings/email endpoint uses @login_optional instead of @login_required. An unauthenticated request reaches set_email with g.uid set to None, so the account-modifying operation runs without authentication. The sibling /settings/password endpoint correctly uses @login_required. The email change is also a common step in account takeover. The handler also hardcodes the new address, but the missing auth check is the flaw.
finding.source: Unauthenticated remote attacker sends POST /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, "new@example.org") at routes.py:37, a protected account-modification operation

trace.note: Decorated with login_optional rather than login_required
g.uid = session.get('uid') evaluates to None when there is no session, and the request continues
set_email(None, ...) is called without any authentication check

finding.guards_checked: login_required is not applied. login_optional never aborts. There is no other auth check, CSRF protection or before_request hook in the file. If set_email handles uid None it could be a no-op, but its body is a stub, and any implementation that falls back to a default or null user would be exploitable. Also, an authenticated user's request has no CSRF token check.

verdict.guard_found: none. login_optional (routes.py:19-25) only sets g.uid = session.get("uid") and never aborts. There is no before_request hook, CSRF check or other auth check in the file. set_email (routes.py:48-49) is a stub with no uid validation.
verdict.reason: routes.py:35 applies login_optional, which at routes.py:22 sets g.uid to None for anonymous requests and never aborts, so routes.py:37 calls set_email(None, ...) with no authentication, unlike /settings/password, which uses login_required (routes.py:11-12); real-world impact depends on the stub set_email at routes.py:48, but the missing auth guard is genuine.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none (login_optional at routes.py:19-25 never aborts; no before_request or other auth check)
verdict_facts.reason: routes.py:35 applies login_optional, which sets g.uid=None without aborting (routes.py:22), so an anonymous POST to /settings/email reaches set_email(None, ...) at routes.py:37, unlike /settings/password, which uses login_required (routes.py:42); set_email is only a stub (routes.py:48-49), so the real impact depends on its implementation.
